Stated Claim / Post Context:
With Trump polling at new lows, FCC chair issues warning about ‘fake polls’ | CNN Business

With numerous reputable polls showing Democrats poised to make big gains in the midterm elections, the Republican chair of the FCC is advising local broadcasters to beware of “fake polls,” without specifying which ones he thinks are bogus.

Actual Article Body:
Markets

Hot Stocks

Fear & Greed Index

Latest Market News

Hot Stocks

With numerous reputable polls showing Democrats poised to make big gains in the midterm elections, the Republican chair of the FCC is advising local broadcasters to beware of “fake polls,” without specifying which ones he thinks are bogus.

Brendan Carr, a close ally of President Donald Trump, warned FCC-licensed stations on Wednesday, the same day two new, highly respected national polls showed Trump registering another record-low approval rating.

His warning also came one day after a self-professed polling firm admitted to being a “fictional entity” that fabricated data and fooled news outlets.

That’s a real — and infuriating — problem, but it shouldn’t besmirch the high-quality polls that are helping inform the electorate.

So which polls was Carr warning about? His X post didn’t say, and he didn’t respond to CNN’s request for comment on Wednesday afternoon, leaving the matter nebulous. And perhaps that was partly the point.

A group of former FCC officials called Carr’s message “part of an accelerating White House strategy to tilt the electoral playing field in the President’s favor and deny election results that don’t go his way.”

The former officials also noted that “the FCC has zero authority to dictate editorial decisions.”

Indeed, Congress has prohibited the FCC from trying to prevent the broadcast of any point of view. But the agency is responsible for licensing local radio and TV stations across the US and upholding basic standards, and Carr has repeatedly used that limited power to pressure broadcasters.

Press advocacy groups argued that Carr’s latest post flew in the face of the First Amendment.

“Literally every time he attacks the press, it’s because of reporting that was unfavorable to his boss, Donald Trump, whose gilded face he’s been known to wear as a lapel pin,” said Seth Stern, the chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation.

Right now there’s a lot of unfavorable reporting about the Republican Party’s electoral prospects, given widespread voter dissatisfaction with the economy and the state of the country.

Trump has defaulted to calling the polls “fake” and has occasionally threatened to match his words with actions. “I’ve been fighting pollsters,” Trump said at a rally on Tuesday.

But if Trump has intended to chill reporting on public opinion, he hasn’t succeeded.

Last month, an Iowa judge dismissed the president’s lawsuit against pollster J. Ann Selzer, her polling company, the Des Moines Register and Gannett. A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team vowed to appeal.

On Wednesday, Carr claimed that this election season has brought “a significant surge in entirely Fake Polls and Suppression Polls designed to do nothing more than interfere with the regular functioning of the electoral process and alter the normal patterns of voter turnout and enthusiasm.”

He said “many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing” the polls, though he didn’t name any polls or names.

Carr then invoked the FCC’s power to penalize stations that violate the agency’s policies against “news distortion” and “hoaxes,” though those policies are narrowly tailored and rarely enforced.

“Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations,” he wrote.

Anna Gomez, the FCC’s lone Democratic commissioner, immediately spoke out against Carr’s message.

“Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong,” Gomez wrote on X. “FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.”

Stern made a similar point in a statement on Wednesday. “News broadcasters have a First Amendment right to report polling data, even if it proves to be inaccurate, just like they have a First Amendment right to report on Carr and Trump’s own countless lies and distortions, even when they turn out to be inaccurate,” he said.

By inveighing against “fake polls,” Carr is once again embracing the rhetoric of the president who appointed him in 2017 and promoted him to chairman last year.

The timing is striking, since the midterm elections are less than two weeks away and polls show Democrats with an edge in many key races.

Many viewers and readers wonder about the reliability of polls, and the reality is that some are more trustworthy than others.

Earlier this week, the poll-tracking site FiftyPlusOne prepared an investigation into a group called “Wedgewood Polls,” which had released more than a dozen election-season polls.

FiftyPlusOne included the group’s data in its polling averages, but found evidence of fabrications. After the poll tracker asked for comment, Wedgewood issued a statement claiming it was an experiment “to demonstrate the vulnerabilities, lack of oversight, and overall low barrier to entry in the modern political polling industry.”

FiftyPlusOne co-founder G. Elliott Morris charged that “they are trying to cover up their fraud with the ‘we were doing a social experiment’ excuse.”

The American Association for Public Opinion Research condemned the fabrication on Wednesday.

“Professional polling organizations are transparent, ethical, and work hard to provide critical information to the public and other stakeholders. It is important that we don’t conflate fraudulent activity like this with legitimate election polling,” the association’s president Mary Losch said.

Even if it was just an experiment, it did real damage, playing right into the hands of public figures who want to sow distrust in even the most authoritative polling sources.

“Fake news, fake polls, they’re all fake,” Trump said Tuesday. He then added in the next breath, “I have some great polls.”

Trump Snaps at ABC News Reporter Over Russia Question

Donald Trump calls an ABC News reporter a “stupid person” after she questions him about Russia sanctions and the release of American detainee Stephen Hubbard.

Actual Article Body:
Trump Snaps at ABC News Reporter Over Russia Question: “You’re a Stupid Person”

Donald Trump insulted an ABC News reporter outside the White House on Wednesday, October 21, after she questioned whether his decision to waive sanctions against Russia amounted to a concession to Moscow. The tense exchange unfolded as journalists pressed Trump about the release of American detainee Stephen Hubbard and his administration’s relationship with Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

Video

When she identified ABC News, Trump responded with a personal insult.

“You’re a stupid person, and by the way, your network is the worst of all.”

Trump’s remarks came shortly after another heated interaction with CNN chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins. According to The Independent, Collins repeatedly questioned Trump about the sanctions waiver and whether it was connected to Hubbard’s release.

Trump responded by calling Collins a dummy, questioning her intelligence and attacking CNN’s credibility. He defended his decision by arguing that enforcing sanctions could have disrupted negotiations with Russia, including efforts to bring Hubbard home and discussions about ending the war in Ukraine.

The dispute centered on a significant diplomatic development.

According to ABC News, Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, was released from Russian detention Wednesday after being held since 2022. Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, traveled to St. Petersburg, where he met with Putin and helped oversee Hubbard’s release.

Hubbard had been detained in eastern Ukraine following Russia’s invasion. Russian authorities accused him of fighting as a mercenary for Ukrainian forces, allegations his legal team disputed. He was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison following closed court proceedings.

The Associated Press reported that the U.S. government previously designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. His release ended more than four years of imprisonment and reunited him with the prospect of returning to his family.

Trump credited his direct communication with Putin for securing Hubbard’s freedom. He maintained that the United States did not have to release another prisoner in exchange.

However, questions remained about the administration’s broader decisions involving Russia, particularly the sanctions waiver that preceded Hubbard’s release.

According to a separate Associated Press report, Trump waived sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act shortly before they were scheduled to take effect. The legislation had received bipartisan congressional support and was intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its continuing invasion of Ukraine.

The move prompted criticism from Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Republican Senators Rick Scott and Thom Tillis publicly challenged the decision, arguing that weakening economic pressure on Russia could undermine efforts to hold Moscow accountable.

Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy also expressed concern about the suspended measures, which were designed to restrict revenue supporting Russia’s war effort.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently indicated that the administration could take up to 60 days to review the economic implications of implementing the sanctions.

Those developments explain why the ABC News reporter pressed Trump about whether suspending the penalties represented a benefit to Russia. Although Trump denied exchanging prisoners or making a direct trade, that denial did not fully address the question of whether the sanctions waiver provided Moscow with an economic or diplomatic advantage.

The confrontation also followed another dispute involving a White House journalist.

On Tuesday, October 20, Trump clashed with Andrew Feinberg, a White House correspondent for The Independent, during an Oval Office appearance. Feinberg had questioned the administration’s proposed fraud whistleblower incentive program and raised additional questions about government policy.

Trump repeatedly ordered Feinberg to be quiet and questioned whether something was wrong with him. The incident added to a documented series of confrontations between Trump and journalists during public appearances.

Her reporting and commentary center on transparency, truth, and the influence of government decisions on daily life.

Following increased public attention and threats tied to her coverage of the administration, she has chosen to maintain a lower public profile while continuing her work. Despite this, her voice remains a consistent and trusted source of insight for readers seeking clarity in an increasingly complex political landscape.

Report: Trump DOJ considers suing more states to control ballot counting, before or after the midterms

California automatically mails ballots to registered voters. Seven other states — Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington — as well as Washington, D.C., also conduct all-mail elections.

Actual Article Body:
By Yunior Rivas

October 21, 2026

to see more of our voting rights news coverage when you search.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) is considering filing lawsuits against additional states before or after the midterms as part of its effort to force states to investigate alleged noncitizens on their voter rolls, according to an NBC News report.

A DOJ official involved in the investigations told NBC News that the department is looking at states that automatically send mail ballots to registered voters, though the official would not identify which specific states could face lawsuits.

The revelation comes less than a week after the Trump administration sued California and Los Angeles County, demanding that election officials set aside ballots belonging to thousands of people federal agencies have identified as likely noncitizens until their citizenship can be verified.

Join 350,000 readers who rely on our daily and weekly newsletters for the latest in voting, elections and democracy.

California automatically mails ballots to registered voters.

Seven other states — Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington — as well as Washington, D.C., also conduct all-mail elections.

The DOJ official said the department plans to continue pushing California to segregate the disputed ballots and believes it can do so for 30 days after Election Day, while counties continue certifying election results.

The official would not say whether DOJ would seek to delay certification in California or in other states that could face similar lawsuits.

That possibility would mark a significant escalation in the Trump administration’s efforts to intervene in state election administration as voting is already underway.

DOJ’s California lawsuit is already facing intense scrutiny over the reliability of the federal government’s list.

Los Angeles County reviewed a sample of records from the list and found that nearly half were canceled or inactive registrations, more than 70% had no voting history and roughly one in four listed a birthplace in the United States.

The department’s broader effort to identify alleged noncitizen voters has also repeatedly produced false positives.

This summer, the Trump administration claimed nearly 16,000 Nevada voters were potential noncitizens. DHS later narrowed that number to 185, but Nevada officials said state records showed all 185 were citizens.

The possible expansion of DOJ’s litigation campaign comes as the administration ramps up federal investigations of alleged voter fraud ahead of the midterms.

Last month, a senior DOJ official reportedly warned federal prosecutors that they could face termination if they refused to pursue voter fraud investigations referred by the FBI or Department of Homeland Security, though DOJ disputed that account.

Homeland Security Investigations has also launched what internal guidance called a “coordinated criminal voter fraud surge initiative” in nine states, including California, Nevada and Washington.

Report: Trump DOJ considers suing more states to control ballot counting, before or after the midterms

Actual Article Body:
By Yunior Rivas

October 21, 2026

to see more of our voting rights news coverage when you search.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) is considering filing lawsuits against additional states before or after the midterms as part of its effort to force states to investigate alleged noncitizens on their voter rolls, according to an NBC News report.

A DOJ official involved in the investigations told NBC News that the department is looking at states that automatically send mail ballots to registered voters, though the official would not identify which specific states could face lawsuits.

The revelation comes less than a week after the Trump administration sued California and Los Angeles County, demanding that election officials set aside ballots belonging to thousands of people federal agencies have identified as likely noncitizens until their citizenship can be verified.

California automatically mails ballots to registered voters.

Seven other states — Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington — as well as Washington, D.C., also conduct all-mail elections.

The DOJ official said the department plans to continue pushing California to segregate the disputed ballots and believes it can do so for 30 days after Election Day, while counties continue certifying election results.

The official would not say whether DOJ would seek to delay certification in California or in other states that could face similar lawsuits.

That possibility would mark a significant escalation in the Trump administration’s efforts to intervene in state election administration as voting is already underway.

DOJ’s California lawsuit is already facing intense scrutiny over the reliability of the federal government’s list.

Los Angeles County reviewed a sample of records from the list and found that nearly half were canceled or inactive registrations, more than 70% had no voting history and roughly one in four listed a birthplace in the United States.

The department’s broader effort to identify alleged noncitizen voters has also repeatedly produced false positives.

This summer, the Trump administration claimed nearly 16,000 Nevada voters were potential noncitizens. DHS later narrowed that number to 185, but Nevada officials said state records showed all 185 were citizens.

The possible expansion of DOJ’s litigation campaign comes as the administration ramps up federal investigations of alleged voter fraud ahead of the midterms.

Last month, a senior DOJ official reportedly warned federal prosecutors that they could face termination if they refused to pursue voter fraud investigations referred by the FBI or Department of Homeland Security, though DOJ disputed that account.

Homeland Security Investigations has also launched what internal guidance called a “coordinated criminal voter fraud surge initiative” in nine states, including California, Nevada and Washington.
